judge_panel.reason: The paper only compares fixed and random resets on the 2D benchmark (Section 5.1), and on circuit tasks the RL Backbone uses a fixed reset point. There is no circuit-level ablation isolating random resets, different k/m/n/N_update values, selection from S vs P, or Phase-2-only variants. The paper states 'RL Backbone, our foundational reinforcement learning system, which starts episodes from a fixed point' but never ablates alternatives on actual circuits.

The paper’s circuit comparisons use only BO, a fixed-start RL backbone, and RoSeOpt variants: “(2) RL Backbone, our foundational reinforcement learning system, which starts episodes from a fixed point; (3) RoSeOpt...” while the only explicit fixed-vs-random reset ablation appears in the toy study: “After training our Lighthouse RL method and RL backbones with fixed and random reset points for 12,000 time steps...” No circuit-task ablation of random resets, Phase 2, or lighthouse-selection choices is reported.

The paper restricts its ablation of reset strategies (fixed vs. random vs. lighthouse) to the 2D benchmark in Section 5.1 and Figure 2, but for the circuit tasks in Sections 5.2 and 5.3, the only RL baseline provided is the 'RL Backbone, our foundational reinforcement learning system, which starts episodes from a fixed point'. The reviewer accurately points out the absence of ablations on the circuit tasks.

general.reason: The paper claims 'the proposed reset strategy can be integrated with any RL-based black-box optimization approach without modifying the underlying algorithm, making our approach a plug-and-play enhancement to existing algorithms,' yet all experiments use a single SAC-based backbone across one toy benchmark and two analog circuits. No other RL algorithm or black-box domain is tested, so the broad claim exceeds the empirical evidence provided.

evidence.claim: The broad claim that the reset strategy works for any RL-based or black-box optimization approach is not substantiated, as experiments only demonstrate one SAC-based implementation and three environments.
evidence.excerpt: The broad “plug-and-play” / “any RL-based optimization approach” scope is stronger than the evidence. The abstract, Sec. 1, Sec. 4.2, and Conclusion state that the reset strategy can be integrated with any RL-based black-box optimization approach and applies to general black-box optimization problems. The experiments only demonstrate one SAC-based implementation with one toy benchmark and two analog circuits. This supports promise, but not broad algorithm-agnostic validity across RL families or black-box domains.

judge_panel.reason: The paper claims 'the proposed reset strategy can be integrated with any RL-based black-box optimization approach without modifying the underlying algorithm, making our approach a plug-and-play enhancement to existing algorithms,' yet all experiments use a single SAC-based backbone across one toy benchmark and two analog circuits. No other RL algorithm or black-box domain is tested, so the broad claim exceeds the empirical evidence provided.

The scope claim is broad: “The proposed reset strategy can be integrated with any RL-based black-box optimization approach without modifying the underlying algorithm” and “the Lighthouse RL approach applies to general black-box optimization problems.” But the evidence is limited to one algorithm family—“We chose SAC...” —and experiments on “a simple 2D multi-objective feasibility problem” plus “two analog circuits,” so the paper does not substantiate algorithm-agnostic or domain-general validity.

The paper frequently claims its strategy is a 'plug-and-play enhancement for any RL-based optimization approach' (Abstract, Section 1, Conclusion), yet only implements and tests it with Soft Actor-Critic ('We chose SAC because...', Section 2.3), making the reviewer's critique of the overbroad claim accurate.
